stem: The primary benefit of design patterns is:
options: A shared VOCABULARY - 'use a factory here' replaces a paragraph
explanation: A pattern is a named, proven solution to a recurring problem. The name is the point: designers can discuss structure in single words.

stem: Basket.Checkout(IDiscount discount) with NoDiscount / PercentageDiscount / StudentDiscount is which pattern?
options: Strategy - swap the algorithm at run time
explanation: Interchangeable behaviours behind one interface. You have used it all course: List.Sort(comparison) and Where(predicate) are Strategy.

options: HOW enemies are constructed - one place to change or extend creation
explanation: Game code never says new Dragon(). Change how dragons are built, or add a Lich, and only the factory is touched.

stem: Which C# language feature IS the Observer pattern built in?
explanation: Publisher announces, subscribers react, neither knows the other - += / -= and ?.Invoke are Observer with language support.

stem: Why is Singleton 'the most over-used pattern'?
options: It is GLOBAL STATE in disguise: hard to test, hides dependencies, threading hazards
explanation: Almost always you actually want ONE instance created at startup and INJECTED (2.13 D) - visible, swappable, testable. Recognise Singleton; use it rarely.

stem: IBookRepository with InMemory / Sql / Json implementations hides what from callers?
options: WHERE the data lives - storage is swappable without touching business code
explanation: Repository is Strategy applied to storage. Project 7.4's ITodoStore is exactly this - and its in-memory fake is the testing payoff.

stem: When do you reach for an Adapter?
options: When you CANNOT CHANGE the other class - a package, a legacy API - and must fit it to your interface
explanation: The adapter translates your interface into calls on the incompatible thing: LegacyLoggerAdapter turns ILogTarget.Write into legacy.WriteEntry(1, ...).

stem: new WithSyrup(new WithMilk(new SimpleCoffee())) beats subclassing because:
options: Every COMBINATION would need its own subclass; wrapping composes any mix at run time
explanation: MilkSyrupExtraShotCoffee, SyrupOnlyCoffee... the class count explodes. Decorators stack. .NET streams work this way: new GZipStream(new FileStream(...)).

stem: foreach over IEnumerable is which classic pattern, built into the language?
explanation: Iterator: sequential access without exposing the underlying structure. Also built-in: events=Observer, delegates-as-parameters=Strategy, streams=Decorator.

stem: The right time to introduce a pattern is:
options: When the SIMPLE version starts to hurt - patterns answer problems you HAVE
explanation: Forcing five patterns into a small program makes it harder to read, not easier. Write the simple version first; reach for the pattern when its pain appears.
